title: Sentence Structure Basics
objectives: Vary sentence length for better writing
target_phrases: These two sentences can be combined with...
This sentence is too long, so...
The subject is... and the verb is...
A better way to write this is...

dialogue.title: Writing Workshop at Work
dialogue.context: Ahmed's supervisor helps him improve his written communication at work by reviewing an email he wrote.

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Ahmed, thanks for sending me that email draft. Let's go through it together to make it clearer.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Sure! I want to improve my writing. What did I do wrong?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Look at this first line: 'Need to order more supplies.' That's a sentence fragment because it doesn't have a subject.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Oh! Should it be 'We need to order more supplies'?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Exactly! A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb. Now look at this one: 'The printer is broken we need a new one the old one is too expensive to fix.'

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: That sounds wrong when I read it out loud. It's too long?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Yes, it's a run-on sentence - actually three sentences combined without proper punctuation. You could write: 'The printer is broken. We need a new one because the old one is too expensive to fix.'

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: So I broke it into two sentences and used 'because' to connect ideas?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Perfect! You're getting it. Here's another tip: vary your sentence length. If all sentences are the same length, writing becomes boring.

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Mix short, clear sentences with longer, more detailed ones. For example: 'The meeting went well. We discussed the new project, reviewed the timeline, and assigned tasks to team members.'

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Oh, I see! Short sentence, then a longer one with more information.

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Exactly! Keep practicing and your writing will improve quickly.

examples: Ahmed writes emails every day.
The team finished the project on time.
She needs more time to complete the report.
We discussed the problem during the meeting.
The manager approved the budget.
I finished the report, and I sent it to my boss.
The deadline is tomorrow, but we're almost done.
We can meet on Monday, or we can reschedule for Tuesday.
The printer broke, so we ordered a new one.
She studied hard, and she passed the test.
We need a new printer because the old one is broken.
I'll finish the report when I have more information.
Although it's difficult, I'm learning to write better.
If you need help, please ask your supervisor.
She arrived late because there was traffic.

listening_exercises.transcript: A complete sentence must have a subject and a verb, and it must express a complete thought. Fragment: 'Running to the store.' This has a verb but no clear subject or complete thought. Complete: 'I am running to the store.' This has a subject (I), verb (am running), and complete thought. Always check: Can this stand alone as a complete idea?
listening_exercises.question: What must a complete sentence have?

listening_exercises.transcript: Run-on sentences happen when you connect multiple sentences without proper punctuation or conjunctions. Wrong: 'I went to the store I bought milk I came home.' Right: 'I went to the store, bought milk, and came home.' Or: 'I went to the store. I bought milk. Then I came home.' Use periods, semicolons, or conjunctions to fix run-ons.
listening_exercises.question: How can you fix a run-on sentence?

listening_exercises.transcript: Three sentence types: Simple sentences have one subject and verb. Compound sentences join two independent clauses with conjunctions. Complex sentences have one independent clause and one dependent clause. Example: Simple - 'She runs.' Compound - 'She runs, and he walks.' Complex - 'She runs because she enjoys exercise.' Varying sentence types makes writing more interesting.
listening_exercises.question: What is a compound sentence?

speaking_tasks.prompt: Explain the difference between a complete sentence and a fragment. Give one example of each. Record for 25 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: A complete sentence has a subject, a verb, and expresses a complete thought. For example: 'Ahmed writes emails at work.' This has a subject (Ahmed), a verb (writes), and a complete idea. A fragment is incomplete. For example: 'Writing emails at work.' This has a verb form but no clear subject and doesn't express a complete thought. To fix this fragment, I could write 'I am writing emails at work' or 'Ahmed is writing emails at work.' Understanding this difference helps you write more clearly.

speaking_tasks.prompt: Take this run-on sentence and explain how to fix it: 'I woke up I ate breakfast I went to work I had a meeting.' Record for 20 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: This is a run-on sentence because it connects four separate ideas without proper punctuation or conjunctions. To fix it, I could break it into separate sentences: 'I woke up. I ate breakfast. Then I went to work and had a meeting.' Or I could use conjunctions: 'I woke up, ate breakfast, and went to work, where I had a meeting.' Both ways are correct and clearer than the run-on.

writing_tasks.prompt: Fix these fragments and run-ons. Then rewrite them as correct sentences: 1) 'Need more time.' 2) 'The project is done we finished early it was easier than expected.' (50-70 words)
writing_tasks.example:
Here are the corrected sentences:

1) Fragment: 'Need more time.' Fixed: 'I need more time to complete the assignment.' This now has a subject (I), a verb (need), and expresses a complete thought.

2) Run-on: 'The project is done we finished early it was easier than expected.' Fixed: 'The project is done. We finished early because it was easier than expected.' I broke the run-on into two sentences and used 'because' to show the relationship between the ideas.

writing_tasks.prompt: Write 5 sentences about your daily routine. Use a mix of simple, compound, and complex sentences. (60-80 words)
writing_tasks.example: I wake up at 6 AM every day. I exercise for 30 minutes before breakfast because it gives me energy for the day. After breakfast, I go to work, and I usually arrive by 8 AM. Although my job is challenging, I enjoy working with my team. We have meetings in the morning, and then I work on my projects. When I finish work at 5 PM, I go home and spend time with my family. This routine helps me stay organized and productive.

grammar_focus.title: Simple, Compound, and Complex Sentences
grammar_focus.explanation: Simple = one independent clause. Compound = two independent clauses joined. Complex = independent + dependent clause.
examples: She works. (simple: one independent clause)
She works, and he studies. (compound: two independent clauses)
She works because she needs money. (complex: independent + dependent)
When it rains, we stay inside. (complex: dependent + independent)

practice.sentence: I eat lunch. (This is a ___ sentence)
I eat lunch, and she drinks coffee. (This is ___)
I eat lunch when I'm hungry. (This is ___)

grammar_focus.title: Conjunctions for Combining Sentences
grammar_focus.explanation: Use FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) to join independent clauses with a comma.
examples: I was tired, so I went to bed. (result)
She studied, but she didn't pass. (contrast)
We can walk, or we can drive. (choice)
He's smart, and he's kind. (addition)

practice.sentence: She can call, ___ she can text.

grammar_focus.title: Subordinating Conjunctions for Complex Sentences
grammar_focus.explanation: Use words like because, although, when, if, since to create dependent clauses.
examples: I stayed home because I was sick. (reason)
Although it's cold, I'll go outside. (contrast)
When she arrives, we'll start. (time)
If you need help, ask me. (condition)

cultural_notes: In American business writing, clear, concise sentences are highly valued. Avoid overly long, complex sentences.
Email writing in the U.S. tends to be direct and brief. Short, clear sentences work best.
Academic writing in American universities values varied sentence structure - mix simple and complex sentences.
Professional editors often recommend the 'one idea per sentence' rule for clarity.
Grammar-checking tools like Grammarly are widely used in American workplaces.
Many Americans learn the 'FANBOYS' acronym (For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So) for coordinating conjunctions.
